newsitem.title: ITALY: Ousland says Antarctica trek feat fulfils a dream.
newsitem.headline: Ousland says Antarctica trek feat fulfils a dream.

text.p: Norwegian explorer Borge Ousland, the first person to cross Antarctica on foot, alone and unaided, said on Monday he was tired but very happy and relieved to have fulfilled the dream of his life.

Following some of the route taken in 1911 by countryman Roald Amundsen, the first person to reach the South Pole, Ousland travelled 2,840 km (1,700 miles) across the world's coldest continent in the longest polar trek ever accomplished. He reached the South Pole on December 19.
Ousland, 34, arrived at New Zealand's Scott Base on the Pacific coast of Antarctica at 2345 GMT on January 17 after leaving Berkner Island in the Weddell Sea on November 15.
"I'm extremely happy to have achieved this goal, the most important goal of my life," he told reporters in a telephone link between Scott Base and the Milan office of his sponsors.
"Now I look back it's almost unreal it's happened - it's a great relief to have fulfilled a dream with something that's never been done before. Only now I realise what a feat it was.
"The first thing I did when I arrived at the base was to phone my wife Wenche in Oslo and she said, 'Well, I told you you would do it'," Ousland said.
"My expedition shows it is still possible to break frontiers of human endurance in a plastic world where nowadays there are few genuine things to do," he said.
Dragging a 180-kg (430-lb) sled with provisions, Ousland used skis and "para-wing" sails to speed him on the journey amid temperatures as low as minus 50 degrees Celsius (-58F).
A deep-sea diver on North Sea oilfields by trade, he had already become the first person to reach both of the Earth's poles alone without the aid of dogs, motorised transport or air-dropped supplies.

On April 22, 1994, he reached the North Pole after 52 days and 970 km (580 miles) alone. On December 21, 1995, during his first attempt to cross Antarctica, he completed a trek of 1,325 km (825 miles) to the South Pole before frostbite forced him to give up nine days later.

"This time I set off better prepared physically and mentally, with much greater respect for Antarctica and a much more humble attitude. Frostbite was not a real problem, I was much more careful," he said.
"Antarctica is an extreme place with very strong winds, extreme temperatures and high altitude. But the greatest danger was the crevasses - I've crossed more crevasses than I can count."

He said he followed a strict discipline, skiing for 10 hours a day with regular breaks and sleeping eight hours at night. "When I got in the tent I could then enjoy a meal of freeze-dried meat and mashed potatoes and read or listen to some music tapes." He lost 15 kg (36 lb) in weight during his trek.
"The mental aspect is very important when you're on your own and there is always the possibility of losing motivation. I set myself short goals. Every hour and every day is a victory."

Ousland did not yet know when he would be returning home to Oslo. He said New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger had offered him a place on his plane to return to Christchurch on Saturday after a ceremony marking the 40th anniversary of the Scott Base.
"The most fascinating aspect of Antarctica is that it is so uncontaminated and untouched by human beings - perhaps the only place on earth that is - I hope it stays that way," he added.
